meta.title: Errors & L1/L2 Learning
meta.randomizationRule: Randomize question selection/order and answer-option order on every attempt; never reuse an exact attempt signature.
meta.alignment: TKT Module 1 — Background to language learning: the role of error, errors and slips, L1 interference, developmental errors, overgeneralisation, interlanguage and fossilisation

questions.prompt: A learner says, “He go to school... sorry, he goes to school.” What type of mistake is this?
questions.correctAnswer: A slip
questions.explanation: A slip is a mistake that the learner can recognise and correct independently.

questions.prompt: A learner repeatedly uses a structure incorrectly and cannot correct it alone. What is this most likely to be?
questions.correctAnswer: An error
questions.explanation: An error reflects language the learner has not yet fully learned or processed.

questions.prompt: Which statement best distinguishes a slip from an error?
options: A slip can usually be self-corrected; an error usually cannot
A slip is always grammatical and an error is always lexical
A slip only occurs in writing
questions.correctAnswer: A slip can usually be self-corrected; an error usually cannot
questions.explanation: Self-correction is the key distinction in TKT terminology.

questions.prompt: A tired B2 learner says, “She have finished”, immediately notices it and says, “Sorry, she has finished.” How should this be classified?
questions.correctAnswer: Slip
questions.explanation: The learner knows the correct form and self-corrects immediately.

questions.prompt: Why are learner errors useful to teachers?
options: They can show what learners know and what they still need to learn
They prove the learner is unmotivated
questions.correctAnswer: They can show what learners know and what they still need to learn
questions.explanation: Errors provide diagnostic information about learners' current language development.

questions.prompt: Which example most clearly shows a slip?
options: A learner says “went” incorrectly once, then corrects it without help
A beginner consistently says “goed” and cannot correct it
A learner applies an L1 word order pattern repeatedly
questions.correctAnswer: A learner says “went” incorrectly once, then corrects it without help
questions.explanation: The learner already knows the correct form and is able to self-correct.

questions.prompt: A learner has never studied the past simple and says, “Yesterday I go to the park.” Which term is most appropriate?
questions.correctAnswer: Error
questions.explanation: The learner is attempting language beyond their current level of control.

questions.prompt: Which teacher comment most strongly suggests a slip rather than an error?
options: “She was tired and corrected herself as soon as I prompted her.”
“She always transfers this pattern from her first language.”
questions.correctAnswer: “She was tired and corrected herself as soon as I prompted her.”
questions.explanation: A learner who can correct the language shows that the underlying knowledge is already available.

questions.prompt: What can teachers learn from systematic learner errors?
options: Which areas may need more teaching or practice
That all learners have the same needs
questions.correctAnswer: Which areas may need more teaching or practice
questions.explanation: Patterns of error can help teachers adapt teaching and identify learner needs.

questions.prompt: Which statement is least accurate?
options: Every learner mistake should automatically be treated as a serious error
Errors can be a natural part of learning
questions.correctAnswer: Every learner mistake should automatically be treated as a serious error
questions.explanation: Teachers need to distinguish slips from more systematic errors and decide whether correction is useful.

questions.prompt: A learner says “I goed home” instead of “I went home”. Which type of error can this illustrate?
questions.correctAnswer: Developmental error
questions.explanation: This kind of error can occur naturally as learners apply developing language rules.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes a developmental error?
options: An error that is a natural part of language development
A mistake caused only by tiredness
questions.correctAnswer: An error that is a natural part of language development
questions.explanation: Developmental errors emerge as learners organise and test language rules.

questions.prompt: Why are developmental errors important?
options: They can show that learners are actively working out how the language system works
They show no learning is happening
They always come directly from L1
questions.correctAnswer: They can show that learners are actively working out how the language system works
questions.explanation: These errors often reflect an evolving internal system rather than simple carelessness.

questions.prompt: Which example is most likely to be developmental?
options: Using an L1 word order exactly in English
A fluent learner makes one accidental typo
questions.correctAnswer: “Two mans” after learning regular plural -s
questions.explanation: The learner is extending a general rule to an irregular form.

questions.prompt: Which feature distinguishes a developmental error from a slip?
options: It reflects the learner's current developing language system
It can always be corrected immediately
questions.correctAnswer: It reflects the learner's current developing language system
questions.explanation: A developmental error is part of the learner's evolving competence, not a momentary lapse.

questions.prompt: A child learning English as an additional language says “comed” for “came”. Which explanation best fits?
questions.correctAnswer: Developmental error
questions.explanation: The learner is applying a developing past-tense rule to an irregular verb.

questions.prompt: Which statement about developmental errors is most accurate?
options: They may disappear as the learner's language develops
They are caused only by first-language interference
questions.correctAnswer: They may disappear as the learner's language develops
questions.explanation: As learners reorganise their language system, many developmental errors disappear.

questions.prompt: Which learner behaviour most strongly indicates a developmental process?
options: Applying a productive rule too widely while building the system
Making one typo because of fatigue
Choosing informal language in a formal email
questions.correctAnswer: Applying a productive rule too widely while building the system
questions.explanation: This shows active rule-building during language development.

questions.prompt: Why should teachers not view all developmental errors as failure?
options: They can be evidence that learners are experimenting with language rules
They mean the syllabus is unnecessary
questions.correctAnswer: They can be evidence that learners are experimenting with language rules
questions.explanation: Errors can reveal active processing and development.

questions.prompt: Which example is least likely to be a developmental error?
options: A learner accidentally writes “teh” for “the” once
questions.correctAnswer: A learner accidentally writes “teh” for “the” once
questions.explanation: A one-off typing mistake is more likely to be a slip than a developmental error.

questions.prompt: A learner uses the grammatical pattern of their first language when speaking English, but the pattern is not correct in English. What is this called?
questions.correctAnswer: L1 interference
questions.explanation: L1 interference occurs when the first language affects performance in the target language.

questions.prompt: Which area can be affected by L1 interference?
questions.correctAnswer: Grammar, lexis or pronunciation
questions.explanation: First-language influence can affect several areas of target-language performance.

questions.prompt: A learner replaces an unfamiliar English sound with the closest sound from their first language. Which factor is most relevant?
questions.correctAnswer: L1 interference
questions.explanation: The learner is drawing on the sound system of the first language.

questions.prompt: Why might learners from different L1 backgrounds make different English errors?
options: Their first languages may influence English in different ways
Errors are unrelated to previous language knowledge
questions.correctAnswer: Their first languages may influence English in different ways
questions.explanation: Different L1 systems can create different transfer patterns.

questions.prompt: Which teacher action is most useful when an error is caused by L1 interference?
options: Help learners notice the contrast between the L1 and English pattern
questions.correctAnswer: Help learners notice the contrast between the L1 and English pattern
questions.explanation: Awareness of the difference can help learners avoid transferring an inappropriate L1 pattern.

questions.prompt: A learner consistently places adjectives after nouns because this is normal in the learner's first language. What is the most likely cause?
questions.correctAnswer: L1 interference
questions.explanation: The learner is transferring an L1 word-order pattern into English.

questions.prompt: Which teacher comment most clearly describes L1 interference?
options: “They use this structure because it works that way in their own language.”
“They know the rule but were tired.”
“They have created a new intermediate system.”
questions.correctAnswer: “They use this structure because it works that way in their own language.”
questions.explanation: The comment directly identifies first-language influence.

questions.prompt: Which statement about L1 interference is most accurate?
options: It can affect both receptive expectations and productive language
It is always negative and never useful
questions.correctAnswer: It can affect both receptive expectations and productive language
questions.explanation: Learners use prior language knowledge in many ways, and some transfer may help while other transfer causes errors.

questions.prompt: A learner says an English word with an L1 sound because English contains a phoneme absent from the learner's first language. Which category best fits?
questions.correctAnswer: L1 interference
questions.explanation: The learner is relying on the first-language sound system.

questions.prompt: Which example is least likely to be caused primarily by L1 interference?
options: A learner says “goed” after learning regular past -ed
A learner transfers L1 word order into English
A learner substitutes an L1 sound for an unfamiliar English sound
questions.correctAnswer: A learner says “goed” after learning regular past -ed
questions.explanation: “Goed” is typically explained by overgeneralisation/development rather than direct L1 transfer.

questions.prompt: A learner says “two mans” after learning that English plurals usually take -s. What is this?
questions.correctAnswer: Overgeneralisation
questions.explanation: The learner applies a general rule in a case where it does not apply.

questions.prompt: Which definition best describes overgeneralisation?
options: Using a learned rule in situations where it is not appropriate
Forgetting a rule because of tiredness
questions.correctAnswer: Using a learned rule in situations where it is not appropriate
questions.explanation: Overgeneralisation happens when a rule is extended too widely.

questions.prompt: A learner says “He throwed the ball.” What is the most likely explanation?
questions.correctAnswer: Overgeneralisation of regular past-tense formation
questions.explanation: The learner applies the regular -ed rule to an irregular verb.

questions.prompt: Why is overgeneralisation often considered developmental?
options: It shows learners are forming and applying rules
It means learners have no grammar knowledge
questions.correctAnswer: It shows learners are forming and applying rules
questions.explanation: Applying a rule too broadly is evidence that a rule has been noticed and internalised at least partially.

questions.prompt: Which example best illustrates overgeneralisation rather than L1 interference?
options: Using an L1 question pattern in English
Pronouncing an English sound as the nearest L1 sound
questions.correctAnswer: “Buyed” for “bought” after learning past -ed
questions.explanation: The learner is extending an English rule to an irregular case.

questions.prompt: A learner says “She can sings.” Which explanation may fit?
questions.correctAnswer: Overgeneralisation of third-person -s
questions.explanation: The learner applies the -s rule where a modal verb requires the base form.

questions.prompt: Which learner error most clearly shows overgeneralisation?
options: Using a direct translation from L1
questions.correctAnswer: “Childs” instead of “children”
questions.explanation: The regular plural rule is being applied to an irregular noun.

questions.prompt: Which statement is most accurate?
options: Overgeneralisation can show partial learning of a rule
Overgeneralisation means the learner has learned no rule
questions.correctAnswer: Overgeneralisation can show partial learning of a rule
questions.explanation: The learner has learned a productive rule but not yet its limits or exceptions.

questions.prompt: A teacher hears “I am knowing the answer.” Which possible explanation is closest to overgeneralisation?
options: The learner is extending present continuous use to a stative verb
The learner is making a spelling slip
The learner is refusing to answer
questions.correctAnswer: The learner is extending present continuous use to a stative verb
questions.explanation: The learner is applying a familiar form in a context where English normally restricts it.

questions.prompt: Which teaching response best addresses overgeneralisation?
options: Show the rule together with important exceptions and contrasting examples
Tell learners never to form rules
questions.correctAnswer: Show the rule together with important exceptions and contrasting examples
questions.explanation: Learners need to refine the limits of the rule they have already begun to form.

questions.prompt: What is interlanguage?
options: A learner's developing version of the target language
questions.correctAnswer: A learner's developing version of the target language
questions.explanation: Interlanguage is the evolving language system a learner constructs while learning.

questions.prompt: Which statement about interlanguage is true?
options: It changes as learners learn more
It is fixed from the first lesson
questions.correctAnswer: It changes as learners learn more
questions.explanation: Interlanguage develops over time as the learner's system is reorganised.

questions.prompt: A learner creates a structure that is neither normal in the first language nor correct in English. Which concept may explain this?
questions.correctAnswer: Interlanguage
questions.explanation: Learners may create intermediate rules as part of their developing language system.

questions.prompt: Why is interlanguage useful for understanding learner errors?
options: It shows that learners build evolving internal systems rather than simply copy language
It means L1 has no influence
questions.correctAnswer: It shows that learners build evolving internal systems rather than simply copy language
questions.explanation: Interlanguage explains systematic patterns in learner language.

questions.prompt: Which description best fits interlanguage?
options: A dynamic system influenced by both prior language knowledge and developing target-language knowledge
questions.correctAnswer: A dynamic system influenced by both prior language knowledge and developing target-language knowledge
questions.explanation: Interlanguage is neither simply L1 nor fully target language; it develops between them.

questions.prompt: A learner regularly uses a self-created grammatical pattern that changes later after more exposure. What does this illustrate?
questions.correctAnswer: Interlanguage
questions.explanation: A changing internal language system is characteristic of interlanguage.

questions.prompt: Which teacher comment best reflects an interlanguage perspective?
options: “This pattern is part of the learner's current developing system.”
questions.correctAnswer: “This pattern is part of the learner's current developing system.”
questions.explanation: Interlanguage treats learner language as systematic and developmental.

questions.prompt: Which statement is most accurate?
options: Interlanguage may contain rules from L1, rules from English and learner-created patterns
Interlanguage is identical for all learners
questions.correctAnswer: Interlanguage may contain rules from L1, rules from English and learner-created patterns
questions.explanation: A learner's developing system can combine several sources of knowledge.

questions.prompt: Why can two learners at the same level have different interlanguage systems?
options: They may have different L1s, experiences and developing hypotheses
All learners should have identical systems
questions.correctAnswer: They may have different L1s, experiences and developing hypotheses
questions.explanation: Learner language develops individually based on prior knowledge and experience.

questions.prompt: Which example best illustrates interlanguage rather than a simple slip?
options: A learner repeatedly uses a stable self-created pattern over several weeks
A learner makes one typo and corrects it
A learner says the correct form immediately
questions.correctAnswer: A learner repeatedly uses a stable self-created pattern over several weeks
questions.explanation: A recurring learner-created pattern is evidence of an organised developing system.

questions.prompt: What is fossilisation?
options: When an incorrect language form becomes habitual and difficult to change
When a learner first meets a new word
questions.correctAnswer: When an incorrect language form becomes habitual and difficult to change
questions.explanation: Fossilisation occurs when an error becomes established in the learner's language.

questions.prompt: A B2 learner has omitted third-person -s for years despite knowing the rule. What may this illustrate?
questions.correctAnswer: A fossilised error
questions.explanation: The incorrect form has become persistent and habitual.

questions.prompt: Why can fossilised errors be difficult to correct?
options: The incorrect pattern has become strongly habitual
The learner has never heard English
They are always caused by spelling
questions.correctAnswer: The incorrect pattern has become strongly habitual
questions.explanation: Repeated use can make the incorrect pattern resistant to change.

questions.prompt: What is one important teacher decision when learners make mistakes?
options: Whether, when and how to correct
Whether to correct every word immediately
questions.correctAnswer: Whether, when and how to correct
questions.explanation: Correction should be selective and related to the learner, task and lesson aim.

questions.prompt: During a fluency activity, what may be a sensible correction choice?
options: Delay some correction until after the activity
Interrupt every sentence for every minor mistake
questions.correctAnswer: Delay some correction until after the activity
questions.explanation: Delayed correction can preserve fluency while still addressing useful language points.

questions.prompt: Which description best fits a fossilised error?
options: A persistent error that has become difficult to change
A mistake the learner instantly self-corrects
questions.correctAnswer: A persistent error that has become difficult to change
questions.explanation: Fossilised errors are entrenched habits in learner language.

questions.prompt: Which correction technique encourages learner autonomy most directly?
questions.correctAnswer: Prompting the learner to self-correct
questions.explanation: Self-correction encourages learners to monitor and retrieve language themselves.

questions.prompt: Which factor should influence whether a teacher corrects immediately?
options: The lesson aim, activity type and effect on communication
Whether the error contains a long word
questions.correctAnswer: The lesson aim, activity type and effect on communication
questions.explanation: Correction decisions depend on pedagogical purpose and communicative context.

questions.prompt: A learner makes the same error repeatedly over a long period despite repeated instruction. Which concept is most relevant?
questions.correctAnswer: Fossilisation
questions.explanation: Persistence over time despite instruction suggests fossilisation.

questions.prompt: Which statement about correction is most accurate?
options: Effective correction is selective and should support learning without unnecessarily blocking communication
Every error must be corrected immediately
questions.correctAnswer: Effective correction is selective and should support learning without unnecessarily blocking communication
questions.explanation: Teachers decide if, when and how to correct depending on the learning goal and context.

matchingSets.instruction: Match each learner-language description with the correct term.

items.example: The learner makes a mistake but can immediately correct it.
The learner says “goed” while developing past-tense rules.
The learner transfers a first-language word order into English.
The learner says “childs” after learning regular plural -s.
The learner develops a changing personal grammatical system.
An incorrect form becomes persistent and difficult to change.

matchingSets.instruction: Match each example with the most appropriate explanation.

items.example: A tired learner says the wrong form once, then self-corrects.
A learner uses a structure not yet under their control and cannot self-correct.
An English sound is replaced by the nearest sound in the learner's first language.
A learner repeatedly uses a self-created pattern that later changes.
A long-standing habitual error is difficult to eliminate.
